title: Cap. 1 subject: Aquinas on reprobation/permission; Calvin not inventor
pass_a_gloss: Indeed Aquinas seems more to incline into that opinion which asserts that reprobation itself in fact preceded the foresight of original sin. For when he says to reprobate is that part of Divine providence which permits some to fail from the end of beatitude, he hints that the permission itself of failing from the means leading unto beatitude flows from reprobation, and therefore is posterior to it according to our mode of understanding. Which if the permission itself of failing follows Reprobation, then much more the foresight of actual defection or fall: for it is foreseen not except from the hypothesis of permission. These things are adduced by me unto this end, not that I adhere to this opinion, but that in passing I may touch the ignorance — shall I say, or malice? — of those who lacerate Calvin or Beza with curses, as if primary authors of this opinion, which among the Scholastics and the Pontificians themselves is no less received than that contrary which places the human being infected with sin as the subject of predestination. And as to Calvin, (as far as I can judge) although he rightly denies foresight of sin to be the cause of predestination or reprobation; yet with Augustine he always established that the consideration of foreseen sin is set opposite to God predestinating or reprobating, as a common condition of the subject. Clear are those words, If by the judgment of death all are liable by natural condition whom the Lord predestines unto death, if from a corrupted mass all are taken, it is no wonder if they lie under damnation. But hear yet clearer ones. After Paul taught that God from a lost mass elects and reprobates whom it seemed good to him, why and how that is done so little profits, that rather growing terrified he breaks forth into that cry, O the depth! Tractate On the eternal predestination of God, page 711. I know Beza, and Zanchi, and other most learned men speak a little more harshly, and postpone altogether the consideration of the corrupted mass to the decree of predestination, yet they never think the damnation of anyone decreed except from presupposed sin.
pass_b_english: Aquinas even seems to lean toward saying reprobation in fact preceded foresight of original sin. When he calls reprobation that part of Divine providence which permits some to fall short of beatitude, he implies that permission to fail from the means that lead to beatitude flows from reprobation — and so, in our way of understanding, is posterior to it. If permission to fail follows reprobation, then foresight of the actual fall follows all the more: it is foreseen only on the hypothesis of permission. I bring this in not because I cling to that opinion, but to touch in passing the ignorance — or malice? — of those who curse Calvin or Beza as if they invented a view no less current among Scholastics and even Pontificians than the contrary view that puts the sin-infected human as predestination's subject. As for Calvin (so far as I can judge): he rightly denies that foresight of sin is the cause of predestination or reprobation; yet with Augustine he always holds that consideration of foreseen sin stands before God as he predestinates or reprobates — as a common condition of the subject. Clear words: If all whom the Lord predestines to death are by natural condition liable to death's judgment, if all are taken from a corrupted mass, no wonder they lie under damnation. Hear clearer still. After Paul taught that God from a lost mass elects and reprobates whom he wills, why and how so little helps that, terrified, he breaks into O the depth! (Tractate on God's eternal predestination, p. 711). Beza, Zanchi, and other learned men speak more harshly and set consideration of the corrupted mass wholly after the decree of predestination — yet they never think anyone's damnation decreed except on presupposed sin.
source_text: Imo videtur Aquinas magis inclinare in illam sententiam, quae asserit ipsam reprobationem de facto antecessisse praevisionem originalis peccati. Nam cum dicit reprobare esse illam partem Divinae providentiae, quae permittit aliquos a fine beatitudinis deficere, innuit ipsam permissionem deficiendi a mediis ad beatitudinem ducentibus fluere a reprobatione, & proinde esse illa posteriorem secundum nostrum modum intelligendi. Quod si ipsa permissio deficiendi sequatur Reprobationem, tum multo magis praevisio actualis defectionis sive lapsus: praevidetur enim non nisi ex hypothesi permissionis. Haec a me in eum finem adducuntur, non quod huic sententiae adhaerescam, sed ut obiter perstringam illorum inscitiam dicam, an malitiam? qui Calvinum aut Bezam lacerant maledictis, quasi primarios autores hujus sententiae, quae inter Scholasticos & ipsos Pontificios non minus recepta est, quam illa contraria, quae ponit hominem peccato infectum subjectum praedestinationis. Atque ad Calvinum quod attinet, (quantum ego possum judicare) quamvis recte neget praescientiam peccati esse causam praedestinationis aut reprobationis; tamen cum Augustino semper statuit, praevisi peccati considerationem obversari Deo praedestinanti aut reprobanti, tanquam communem conditionem subjecti. Clara sunt illa verba, Si judicio mortis obnoxii sunt omnes naturali conditione, quos ad mortem Dominus praedestinat, si ex corrupta massa desumpti sunt omnes, non mirum si damnationi subjacent. Sed adhuc clariora audite. Postquam Paulus Deum ex perdita massa eligere & reprobare quos illi visum est, docuit, quare & quomodo id fiat adeo non expedit, ut potius expavescens in clamorem illum erumpat, O altitudo! Tract. De aeterna Dei praedestinatione, pag. 711. Scio Bezam, & Zanchium, aliosque viros perdoctos paulo durius loqui, & massae corruptae considerationem decreto praedestinationis omnino postponere, nunquam tamen damnationem alicujus decerni putant nisi ex praesupposito peccato.
